assessments.explanation: The paragraph describes the applicants' claim of persecution and harm if returned to Venezuela.
It states that the RPD denied the refugee claim based on an internal flight alternative and introduces the issues.
The paragraph discusses the applicants' challenge to the RPD's finding on the viability of the IFA and legal errors alleged.
It reports the applicants' argument that their hearing was unfair due to ineffective assistance from their consultant.
The court states that the application will be dismissed for the reasons that follow.
The paragraph states the standard of review for the procedural fairness issue as correctness, citing relevant case law.
It explains the two-part test for an internal flight alternative under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
The paragraph details the high threshold for objective unreasonableness in the IFA context, including evidence requirements.
It finds that the record does not support a claim based on two distinct grounds of persecution and discrimination.
The court concludes that the RPD's focus on violence was reasonable given the record, and the applicants' claims were primarily about violence.
The court notes the applicant's statements about fear of violence and discrimination, which the RPD reasonably considered.
The court finds that the applicant's statement about discrimination was not a separate claim requiring detailed analysis.
The court observes that discrimination at the children's school was addressed by the RPD and not a separate issue.
It concludes that the RPD's failure to consider further discrimination risks was not unreasonable.
The court considers whether the applicants' isolation in Maracaibo should have been considered in the second IFA prong.
It states that being the only Arab Muslims in Maracaibo is relevant but not sufficient unless it meets the high threshold of the IFA test.
The paragraph notes the lack of documentation on Muslims in Maracaibo and the absence of evidence meeting the high threshold.
It states that general criminal risks are relevant for section 96 but are excluded under section 97 unless they meet the high threshold.
The court emphasizes that evidence of high criminality is needed to meet the threshold for the second IFA prong.
The paragraph states that no evidence of high criminality in Maracaibo was before the RPD, only general violence in Venezuela.
The court finds that the violence in Venezuela does not reach the very high threshold for the second IFA prong.
The paragraph discusses the murder rate and concludes it does not meet the threshold for excluding an IFA.
It notes that claims about kidnapping were not supported by statistics or record evidence.
The court finds that the level of violence does not meet the high threshold, so the error was not material.
The court summarizes that the applicants' claims focused on violence and discrimination, which the RPD reasonably assessed.
The paragraph states the burden on applicants to prove the high threshold for unreasonableness in living in Maracaibo.
The paragraph states that the submissions by the consultant were inadequate and erroneous.
It claims the consultant was incompetent and that the applicants were prejudiced by this.
The paragraph explains the standard for incompetence and miscarriage of justice in legal proceedings, citing GDB.
It notes that principles from GDB have been applied to IRPA proceedings, citing Memari.
The paragraph states that incompetence only breaches natural justice in extraordinary circumstances under IRPA.
The court concludes that the performance of the consultant did not meet the high standard for incompetence.
It describes the questions the consultant asked, which addressed the core fears of the applicants.
The paragraph states that the consultant addressed issues of police protection and safety in Venezuela.
It notes that the consultant discussed the applicants' beliefs about safety and discrimination in Venezuela.
The paragraph states that the consultant's submission about danger and discrimination was understood by the RPD and was relevant.
The court finds that despite shortcomings, the consultant addressed key issues relevant to the claim.
It states that the record lacked evidence to demonstrate the unreasonableness of living in Maracaibo, even with better advocacy.
The paragraph notes that no significant legal question arises and states the judgment of dismissal.
